context_blurb:
Pass the glow of a thin, hot gas through a prism and it splits into sharp coloured lines, like a barcode, and every element prints its own. Those lines colour neon signs and let astronomers read what stars are made of.

A hot solid, like an old bulb's white-hot filament, glows in every colour at once. A thin gas cannot, because an atom's electrons may sit only at set energy levels. In a neon sign a current knocks electrons up a level; dropping back, each gives off a photon, a packet of light holding exactly the energy it lost. So a neon atom gives off energy only in set amounts, each one colour: its many sharp lines include a bright red one at 640 nanometres. Nothing in the tube burns.

A hydrogen electron on the third level may fall straight to the first, releasing one ultraviolet photon of 12.1 electronvolts, a unit sized for atoms, or stop at the second, releasing a red photon of about 1.9 and then an ultraviolet one of 10.2: again 12.1. Each photon carries off exactly what its electron lost, so one drop or two gives the same total: both routes start and end on the same levels.

Each element's electrons have energy levels spaced in its own way, so the drops between them, and their colours, belong to that element alone. In a burner flame strontium glows crimson, copper blue-green and sodium yellow, and a prism splits each glow into thin lines. The flame's heat only lifts the electrons; it does not choose the colour.

In 1814 Joseph von Fraunhofer, a Munich lens maker, found sunlight's colours crossed by dark lines, the same through different glass, so they were no flaw of the prism. With a prism on a telescope he saw the Sun's lines in the Moon, Venus and Mars, which shine by reflected sunlight, but other lines in Sirius and Castor, though their light passed the same air, prism and lens. So those extra lines were made in the stars themselves, before their light set out.

In 1859 at Heidelberg, Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen built a spectroscope, a prism set up for reading the lines of coloured flames. They burned each metal as half a dozen compounds, from chloride to carbonate, in flames of many fuels, cool and fierce. Whatever the compound or the flame, the lines of every metal stayed in the same places.

In 1835 the philosopher Auguste Comte held that the stars' chemistry could never be known. Yet a sodium flame shines a yellow pair exactly where sunlight has two dark lines, called D. In 1859 Kirchhoff sent bright sunlight through a sodium flame, and the D lines, instead of filling in, grew darker. Sodium gas soaks up light of exactly the energies its electrons can jump by, the very colours it gives off. So, Kirchhoff concluded, sodium lies in the cooler gas above the Sun's glowing surface; Comte had died two years before.

At an eclipse in India in August 1868, Pierre Janssen recorded a yellow line from the Sun's rim, and Norman Lockyer saw it in England that autumn. It sat near sodium's pair but on neither, so Lockyer named its maker helium, from helios, Greek for the Sun. Doubt and mockery followed. Proof came in March 1895, when William Ramsay treated cleveite, a uranium mineral, with acid and collected a gas that glowed with the Sun's yellow line. Helium turned up in natural gas only in 1905.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne read stellar lines with Meghnad Saha's theory of ionization, atoms losing electrons in heat. Astronomers had read a strong line as plenty of an element. But in the hottest stars nearly all hydrogen has lost its electron, and in cooler ones like the Sun nearly all sits on its lowest level, out of visible light's reach; only near 10,000 kelvins, as on Sirius, are many atoms ready to make lines. A line's strength, she found, is set mostly by how hot the star's surface is. Read so, stars are mostly hydrogen and helium.

Henry Norris Russell of Princeton, one of her examiners, held, like most astronomers, that the Sun was made of Earth's elements in much the same proportions. He wrote to her that a millionfold excess of hydrogen over the metals was plainly impossible, and her thesis called its figures almost certainly unreal. He reached her answer by another method in 1929, yet for years got most of the credit.
